column1: # Indicative figures compiled from published ICMR-AMRSN / WHO GLASS / CDSCO / NPPA / NCVBDC patterns. Reconstructed for demonstration. Not for clinical use.

column5: Uncomplicated cystitis in women: 3 days of most agents, 5 for nitrofurantoin. Pyelonephritis 7. Anything longer adds resistance, not cure.
7 days is non-inferior to 14 for uncomplicated gram-negative bacteraemia. S. aureus bacteraemia is the exception — 14 days minimum, longer if endocarditis or a deep focus.
5 days, provided the patient is afebrile and clinically stable for 48 hours. Long courses are the commonest overuse in respiratory medicine.
7 days, including for non-fermenting gram-negatives. Longer courses have not shown benefit and select for resistance.
5-6 days for uncomplicated cellulitis with a good response. Extend only if the response is genuinely slow.
4 days after adequate source control. If the patient is still septic, the answer is a second look at the source, not a longer course.
Soft-tissue infection 7-14 days. Osteomyelitis without resection needs 6 weeks — a different decision entirely.
Drainage and debridement matter more than duration.
10-14 days for pneumococcus, 21 for gram-negative meningitis.
Continue until neutrophil recovery and the patient has been afebrile 48 hours.
7 days for azithromycin, 10-14 for ceftriaxone. Relapse is common if cut short.
